newsitem.title: UK: RTZ-CRA sees most non-ferrous metal prices rising.
newsitem.headline: RTZ-CRA sees most non-ferrous metal prices rising.

text.p: Mining giant RTZ-CRA is looking forward to higher non-ferrous metal prices in 1997 with the likely exception of copper, according to its chief economist Phillip Crowson.
And even copper may outperform some of the more bearish projections doing the rounds, he said.
"I think it's very probable...that the prices of six of the (seven) LME metals will be higher by Christmas than they are now," Crowson told Reuters in an interview.
"And I expect that those six prices next year will be way above certainly the last three or four months' average."
The six contracts he referred to are aluminium, lead, nickel, tin, zinc and aluminium alloy, all traded on the London Metal Exchange (LME) along with copper.
"The exception is copper, but even with copper you've probably got some more fizzing before it finally lies back exhausted," he added.

Copper is the most important of the base metals in terms of RTZ-CRA's performance. The group also produces aluminium, lead and zinc, as well as silver and gold, iron ore and coal, diamonds and other industrial minerals.
Crowson's comments came after RTZ-CRA announced a 22 percent fall in net adjusted earnings during the first half of 1996 to $552 million from $711 million a year earlier.
Sharp falls in copper prices were one of the main factors behind the fall in profits.
Crowson said recent volatility in the world copper markets was mainly a reflection of a tight physical market.

"The main reason is that the underlying physical supply/demand balance is still relatively tight. Until that eases on a sustained basis you are going to see a tight market and also see quite a lot of volatility," he said.

But he said it was also the result of uncertainty over the fate of Sumitomo Corp's position after Sumitomo announced in June that it had run up $1.8 billion losses in unauthorised copper trading by star trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
The full impact of the unwinding of Sumitomo's long positions has yet to be felt, Crowson said.
"All right, Sumitomo may have baled out, and probably has, but those who took the positions over clearly haven't and are obviously managing those positions."
Values are likely to remain well supported in the short term before coming under pressure some time next year when the market is expected to move to a modest surplus, Crowson said.

The medium term for aluminium was more positive, based on rising demand expectations, a reduction in stocks over the last few years, limited investment in new output and flat to declining Russian exports to the West.
Production capacity idled since 1994 in order to run down high inventory levels would also not come back on stream quickly, Crowson said.
"It wouldn't surprise me if in the course of the next 18 months...the aluminium price did not exceed the copper price, and I am not expecting too much of a decline in copper."
Early on Thursday cash copper was indicated at around $1,900 a tonne, while aluminium was trading at around $1,400.
The zinc market was heading for another supply deficit in 1997 after recording shortfalls both in 1995 and 1996.
"If you keep having deficits you run down inventory and people tend to get excited about prices," said Crowson.

The price of lead is already high, but could go higher still particularly if the forthcoming winter is severe. Cold winters and hot summers boost lead demand because they increase consumption in its main market, vehicle batteries.
"If you get a nice hard winter all hell is going to break loose because of the battery market," Crowson said.

He said stocks of tin were returning to "normal" levels after a long period of being too high. Chinese exports were unlikely to match recent high levels and there was little new production due on stream.
"So where is it going to come from? It suggests a price rise," he said.

Finally, Crowson said the nickel price was likely to show a "good rise," although he was less bullish than some commentators because of the weakness in the key stainless steel sector, which consumes two thirds of the world's nickel.
